title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
author: Immanuel Kant
openingText: Ancient Greek philosophy was divided into three sciences: physics, ethics, and logic. This division suits the nature of the subject perfectly. The only improvement we can make is to add the principle on which the division rests, so that we can confirm its completeness and identify its necessary subdivisions correctly.
about:
Kant wrote the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals in 1785, between the first Critique (1781) and the second (1788), as a short, dense preparation for a full moral philosophy he had not yet written. He intended it as the foundation stone — the laying-bare of the principle that any later metaphysics of morals would have to stand on. The book is short, around eighty pages, but it is the most concentrated argument in the modern Western canon for the claim that morality cannot rest on consequences, inclination, or any empirical fact about human beings, and must instead be grounded in pure practical reason.

The argument moves through three Sections, each a 'transition' from one stage of moral knowledge to the next. The Preface frames the task: a metaphysics of morals must be entirely a priori, free of any anthropological or psychological content, because moral laws must hold for every rational being as such. Section I begins from the ordinary moral consciousness of a person who knows the difference between acting from duty and acting from inclination, and works analytically toward the formal principle that lies behind that knowledge. Section II carries the argument from popular moral philosophy up to the metaphysical level, derives the categorical imperative in three formulations — the universal law, humanity as an end in itself, and the kingdom of ends — and shows how all duties follow from a single principle. Section III takes the harder step: showing that the moral law has any grip on a finite rational being at all, which Kant traces to the idea of freedom and the autonomy of the will.

The Groundwork is the founding text of deontological ethics. Every subsequent attempt to ground morality in something other than consequences — Hegel, Rawls, Korsgaard, Habermas, Scanlon — works through Kant's arguments here, either to extend them or to escape them. The categorical imperative has become the most-quoted formula in moral philosophy: act only on that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law. The book is famously difficult, but the difficulty is the argument: Kant is trying to do something almost no philosopher had attempted before — to derive the entire content of morality from the bare form of rational willing.

angleCards.title: The good will and acting from duty.
angleCards.text: Section I opens with one of the most famous sentences in moral philosophy: nothing in the world is good without qualification except a good will. Kant then distinguishes acting from duty from acting in conformity with duty — and argues that only the first carries moral worth.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Kant's argument that moral worth lies in acting from duty rather than from inclination, and decide whether that distinction is as cold as it sounds or doing real work.

angleCards.title: The categorical imperative and its formulations.
angleCards.text: Section II derives the central principle of morality in three formulations: act only on a maxim you could will as a universal law; treat humanity always as an end and never merely as a means; act as a legislating member of a kingdom of ends. The three formulations are meant to be one principle from three angles.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Kant's three formulations of the categorical imperative and see how the universal-law version, the humanity-as-end version, and the kingdom-of-ends version are meant to converge on a single moral test.

angleCards.title: Common moral knowledge vs philosophical knowledge.
angleCards.text: Kant's method is unusual: he begins from the moral knowledge of an ordinary person and works upward to philosophical foundations. Each Section is titled 'Transition from… to…' — common rational moral knowledge to philosophical, popular moral philosophy to metaphysics, metaphysics to a critique of pure practical reason. The argument moves in stages.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how Kant moves from ordinary moral judgement to the metaphysical principles that, on his account, were already implicit in it — and decide whether the stages hang together.

angleCards.title: Freedom and the autonomy of the will.
angleCards.text: Section III is the hardest part of the book. Having derived the categorical imperative, Kant has to show that any finite rational being is actually bound by it. His answer turns on freedom — and on the claim that the same will that makes the moral law also gives the law to itself. Autonomy, not heteronomy, is the keystone of moral worth.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Kant's argument in Section III for the link between freedom, autonomy, and moral obligation — and see whether his case for why we are bound by the moral law actually closes.

cast.name: The Good Will
cast.description: The first sentence of Section I: 'Nothing in the world — or even outside it — can possibly be conceived as good without qualification, except a good will.' Talents, courage, wealth, even happiness can be turned to bad ends; only a good will is good in itself, regardless of what it accomplishes. Kant means this as a claim ordinary moral consciousness already recognises. The whole book is an attempt to make explicit what we are already committed to when we praise a good will.

cast.name: The Categorical Imperative
cast.description: Kant's name for the form a moral law must take: a command that holds unconditionally, without reference to any end the agent happens to want. He states it three times in Section II. The universal-law formulation: 'Act only on that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' The humanity formulation: 'Act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in another, always as an end and never merely as a means.' The kingdom-of-ends formulation: act as a legislating member of a community of rational beings each treating each other as ends. Kant claims the three are one principle viewed three ways.

cast.name: The Hypothetical Imperative
cast.description: A command that holds only on a condition: if you want X, do Y. 'If you want to be healthy, exercise.' 'If you want the deal, do not lie.' Hypothetical imperatives have no moral force on their own — they only tell you what to do given an end you already happen to want. Kant introduces them in Section II as the contrast against which the categorical imperative is defined. Most of what we usually call practical advice is hypothetical. Only the categorical kind is properly moral.

cast.name: Duty
cast.description: For Kant, an action has moral worth only when done from duty — that is, from respect for the moral law itself, not from inclination, self-interest, or even sympathetic feeling. He gives examples in Section I: a merchant who deals honestly because honesty is good for business acts in conformity with duty but not from duty. A person who helps others because it gives them pleasure acts from inclination. Only the agent who acts because the action is right, even against inclination, has performed a morally worthy act on Kant's strict definition.

cast.name: Autonomy
cast.description: The will's giving the law to itself. A heteronomous will takes its law from outside — from God's commands, social custom, the pursuit of happiness, the calculation of consequences. An autonomous will recognises the moral law as its own law because reason, which is what the agent essentially is, gives it. Kant argues in Section III that only an autonomous will can be free in the morally relevant sense, and only a free will can be subject to the categorical imperative. The concept of autonomy is the bridge between freedom and morality in the whole Kantian framework.

cast.name: Immanuel Kant
cast.description: A German philosopher (1724–1804), professor at the University of Königsberg, the great systematiser of the Enlightenment. He published the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781 at the age of fifty-seven, after a decade of philosophical silence; the Groundwork followed in 1785, the Critique of Practical Reason in 1788, and the Critique of Judgement in 1790. He never married, never travelled far from Königsberg, and was famous for the regularity of his daily walks. The Groundwork was meant as a brief, accessible preparation for the moral philosophy he would lay out at length in the second Critique and in the much later Metaphysics of Morals (1797).

whyItMatters.title: The Categorical Imperative as a Moral Test
whyItMatters.body: The Groundwork hands moral philosophy a portable instrument. Before acting, ask whether the maxim of the action — the principle on which you are about to act — could be willed as a universal law without contradiction. The maxim 'I will make a lying promise when it is convenient' fails the test: a world in which everyone made lying promises at their convenience would be a world in which promising itself broke down, and so the maxim destroys the practice it relies on. Kant offers four worked examples in Section II, covering suicide, lying promises, neglect of talents, and refusal to help others, and treats them as a demonstration that the imperative actually decides cases. The test is not a calculation of consequences and not an appeal to feeling; it is a check on whether the agent could coherently will the principle of the action as a law for everyone. Two and a half centuries later, the universalisation test still shows up in arguments about everything from contractual ethics to AI alignment.

whyItMatters.title: Deontology Versus Consequences
whyItMatters.body: Almost every modern moral debate breaks along a fault line the Groundwork opened: do we judge actions by their consequences or by the principle on which they are done? Kant's answer is uncompromising. A good consequence achieved by a wrong principle does not redeem the principle, and a bad consequence following from acting on the right principle does not impugn it. He argues this hardest in the case of the lying promise: even if the lie would relieve someone's distress, it remains incompatible with treating that person as an end in themselves. Mill, Bentham, Sidgwick, and the entire utilitarian tradition write against this position; Rawls, Korsgaard, Scanlon, and the entire contemporary Kantian tradition write to refine and defend it. The bioethics, business ethics, and AI ethics literatures all replay the Groundwork's split between treating persons as bearers of dignity and weighing them as variables in an outcome. The fault line was drawn here.

whyItMatters.title: Autonomy as the Ground of Moral Worth
whyItMatters.body: Section III is the part of the Groundwork that does the heaviest philosophical work and the part most modern readers skip. Kant's claim is that a finite rational being can only be bound by a moral law it gives to itself. If the law came from outside — from God's command, social convention, the natural desire for happiness — then obedience would be heteronomous and the agent would not be the genuine source of the moral act. Only autonomy, the will's legislating the moral law to itself, makes moral worth intelligible. From this Kant gets the modern conception of human dignity: persons are not to be used merely as means because they are themselves sources of moral law. The connection between autonomy and dignity in current debates about consent, paternalism, and rights traces directly back to the closing pages of this book.
